Start a 6–8 week plan of tight sleep timing: limit time in bed to about 5 hours for now, keep a fixed wake time each day, leave bed if awake >20 minutes, avoid naps until sleep consolidates, cut caffeine after 14:00, elevate your head-of-bed and avoid late large meals for reflux, add 30 minutes brisk walking most days, and aim for slow weight loss while checking blood pressure/meds with your clinician.

## What your sleep points to
Your study shows short total sleep time (TST 269.5 minutes), low sleep efficiency (SE 55.9%), near-absent REM, and a mild AHI (14.7 events/h). These findings fit an insomnia pattern and flag future risks to watch and prevent: **Insomnia**, **Sleep disorders**, **Anxiety disorder**, **Obesity**, and **Essential hypertension** — each can disturb nights or be worsened by poor sleep and so matter for your plan.

## How the plan addresses these
Limiting time in bed and keeping a strict wake time (then increasing time in bed by 15–20 minutes after several nights of SE >85%) targets **Insomnia** and broader **Sleep disorders** by strengthening sleep drive and timing; leaving bed if awake >20 minutes and removing stimulating activities from bed targets **Insomnia** and **Anxiety disorder** by breaking the bed–wake association; cutting late caffeine, daily 30-minute brisk walks, and slow weight loss target **Obesity** and will also improve sleep continuity; head‑of‑bed elevation and no large meals 2–3 hours before bed aim at reflux that fragments sleep; review of blood‑pressure medicines and monitoring addresses **Essential hypertension** that can affect sleep. The behavioural steps above are supported by systematic evidence for structured behavioural insomnia treatment [1].
